text.p: Several hundred Jamaicans lined up at the National Arena early Friday to be the first to mark the official three-day mourning period for former Prime Minister Michael Manley, who died on March 6.

The opening procession for public viewing of Manley's body was led by Prime Minister P.J. Patterson, cabinet ministers, other politicians, schoolchildren, nurses in uniform, athletes in warm-up jackets and a street-cleaning crew.
Many members of the public came to the viewing in their Sunday best. A small group from Manley's People's National Party held a banner reading, "Michael Manley -- champion of the poor."
Manley's flag-draped wooden coffin was surrounded by plants and flowers, and the walls of the arena were draped in black, gold and green bunting.
Songs sung by a children's choir alternated with solemn classical music. The Jamaica defence and police forces mounted an honour guard.

Manley died at home, aged 72, after a long struggle with cancer. Tributes have come from labourers, communists and monarchs in honour of a man considered a father of Caribbean independence and a champion of working people and Third World rights.
Britain's Queen Elizabeth expressed her condolences to Manley's family, and Cuban President Fidel Castro mourned the loss of a "personal friend."

A state funeral was scheduled for Sunday afternoon, and Manley was to be interred at National Heroes Circle, next to former prime minister Sir Donald Sangster, a distant relative, and near his father Norman, his mother Edna, and his cousin former prime minister Sir Alexander Bustamante.

Jamaican officials have not released a list of dignitaries expected to attend the funeral, citing security concerns. Those expected to come included Castro, former U.S. President Jimmy Carter and former Canadian prime minister Pierre Trudeau.
